title: AI-assisted legal research with cited answers, checked against sources before use
problem: Research memos need accurate answers with valid sources, but AI research tools can invent or misstate authority and vendors' claims have been hard to check.
approach: Lawyers use AI tools for research and first orientation; Deutsche Telekom's general counsel and a Gleiss Lutz partner use Harvey.
Lawyer reads each cited authority and checks each conclusion before it goes into advice or a filing.
Vals study, October 2025: AI products scored 74%-78% against a lawyer baseline of 69% (independent).
Stanford's 2024 test found two leading providers' research tools hallucinated between 17% and 33% of the time (independent).
who: Deutsche Telekom, Gleiss Lutz, Vals, Stanford

title: Summaries, chronologies, transcript analysis and first-pass translation over large record sets
problem: Summarising long records, building chronologies and reading transcripts take much orientation time, and foreign-language documents wait for colleagues or outside translators.
approach: Tools summarise documents and transcripts, draft chronologies and translate first-pass; Grant Thornton UK's forensic team uses Legora for translation and email summaries.
Each AI translation gets a quality check, and a lawyer checks key dates and source references in a chronology.
Vals, February 2025: on summarisation, CoCounsel scored 77.2% against a lawyer baseline of 50.3% (independent).
Chronology generation matched the lawyer baseline at best (80.2%) (independent).
who: Grant Thornton UK, Legora, Vals

title: Bulk extraction of clauses and fields, with cited answers over document sets
problem: Pulling clauses, dates and fields out of long agreements and answering questions across document sets is repetitive manual reading, and quality varies between reviewers.
approach: Tools extract requested fields and answer questions over document sets with citations; users include Goodwin, Dentsu, CMS and A&O Shearman.
Reviewer checks extracted fields against the source text through the returned citations, with spot checks on multi-clause questions.
Vals, February 2025: document Q&A scored up to 94.8% (Harvey Assistant) against a lawyer baseline of 70.1% (independent).
On the hardest extraction question, results varied widely and the lawyer baseline was low at 39.2% (independent).
who: Goodwin, Dentsu, CMS, A&O Shearman, Vals

title: Idea-stage regulatory horizon scanning that feeds advice
problem: Tracking regulatory change across jurisdictions is a continuous reading task done by people and bulletins; this is an announced plan, with no published results.
approach: Hogan Lovells Cadwalader will be a design partner for Legora's Monitors, guiding sources, jurisdictions and alert logic for its global regulatory practice.
BMW Group's legal teams plan to use AI-supported workflows to monitor regulatory developments.
Practice lawyers decide which alerts matter and what to advise. No outcome figure published (vendor-published).
who: Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, BMW Group, Legora

title: First drafts from approved precedents and standards, edited by the lawyer
problem: Drafting clauses, memos and agreements from scratch repeats earlier work, and consistency with approved language depends on who drafts.
approach: Lawyers use AI for initial drafts from approved precedents; Goodwin lists drafting among its Legora uses, and BMW Group plans precedent-based drafts.
Lawyer edits and approves every draft before it leaves the firm or department.
ILTA reports 94% of 508 responding firms engaged with GenAI, up 14 points year on year (independent).
BMW's general counsel says Legora expands in-house capacity; no measurement given (vendor-published).
who: Goodwin, BMW Group, Gleiss Lutz, ILTA

title: Randomised trial of an AI drafting assistant and lawyers' own skill
problem: Drafting complex documents is slow, skilled work, and firms do not know whether AI raises quality or weakens the expertise lawyers build by drafting themselves.
approach: A preregistered trial had 133 patent lawyers at eleven US IP firms use an AI drafting assistant for three months, scored blind.
Blinded scores rose +0.34 SD at 10 days and +0.38 SD at 90 days, more for juniors (vendor-published; Google-funded).
Tested without AI, seniors redlined better than controls (+0.45 SD); juniors showed no average gain (vendor-published).
Lawyer revises and owns the draft; a first draft is never the final submission.
who: Eleven US IP firms; Google-funded study

title: Consulting analysis and first drafts with AI, and which tasks stay human-first
problem: Consultants spend much early-career time on research, data work and first-draft slides, and cannot easily tell which tasks AI helps and which it makes worse.
approach: Consultants use GenAI for research briefs, first drafts and early analysis, then validate it; managers keep judgment-heavy tasks human-first with extra checks.
A Harvard Business School experiment with 758 BCG consultants found 12.2% more tasks completed and 25.1% faster within AI's capability (independent).
On one task outside AI's capability, AI users were 19% less likely to be correct (independent).
A qualified reviewer checks AI-influenced analysis before client release.
who: BCG consultants (HBS study), Deloitte Australia

title: Playbook-based first-pass contract review with suggested edits as tracked changes in Word
problem: Reviewing counterparty paper clause by clause against preferred and fallback positions is slow and repetitive, and the playbook often lives in people's heads.
approach: An agent in Word reviews an agreement against a playbook and proposes tracked-change edits with citations; the lawyer accepts or rejects each.
Microsoft telemetry: users kept about 70% of Legal Agent suggestions, across nearly 100,000 edits and over 1,800 users (vendor-published).
Vals, February 2025: lawyer baseline beat the tools on open-ended redlining, 79.7% against 59.4% for Harvey Assistant (independent).
Lawyer reviews each change before it goes out; terms outside playbook authority are escalated.
who: Microsoft, GE Aerospace, Harvey, Vals

title: AI as a sparring partner that challenges a draft position
problem: Authors have blind spots in their own arguments, and a full adversarial read takes hours of colleagues' time.
approach: O'Melveny's Los Angeles managing partner asks Harvey what opposing counsel is likely to argue about a draft motion to dismiss.
An O'Melveny real estate partner checks how often a provision appears in a lender's last 100 loans before calling it market standard.
A Bracewell partner uses Legora to test ideas. The partner decides which counter-arguments are credible; no measurement published (self-reported).
who: O'Melveny, Bracewell

title: Idea: challenger role and unaided-reasoning check for AI-structured team work
problem: Idea, not a deployment: a coherent AI-structured draft invites continuation rather than challenge, so teams can approve work no one has independently reasoned through.
approach: Idea. Thomson Reuters Legal proposes assigning challengers and having team members state the reasoning in their own words.
It also proposes returning to primary sources and asking whether the team could defend the analysis without AI.
A challenger reviews framing and omissions before finalising. Practitioner proposal; no measurement found (vendor-published).
who: No named deployment

title: Pre-release check of citations, quotations and consistency in AI-assisted documents
problem: AI can produce fluent text citing authorities or reports that do not exist, and fabricated references have reached courts and clients.
approach: Before release, every authority, quotation, reference and figure is checked against its source and a named person records the check.
Grant Thornton UK's forensic team uses Legora as an extra layer; it flagged one date inconsistent with the documented timeline (self-reported).
A live database lists 2,202 court decisions involving hallucinated content (independent); this is the failure scale, not a check result.
Existing multi-reviewer quality control remains the control; a supervising lawyer confirms the check ran.
who: Grant Thornton UK, Legora, Deloitte Australia

title: AI-assisted review of whole document sets in due diligence and portfolio review
problem: Diligence means reading hundreds or thousands of documents on a deadline, and teams that sample or split work by hand can miss issues or find them late.
approach: Teams load the data room into a tool that reads all documents and produces abstracts, issue lists and checklists.
O'Melveny used Harvey on a new property portfolio, surfacing entitlements the client had not known about; lease abstract reviews 'compressed significantly' (self-reported).
CMS says it can review much larger document sets (self-reported). PwC and IFS build diligence analysis in a shared workspace.
Specialist lawyers review flagged issues and sign the diligence memo.
who: O'Melveny, CMS, PwC, IFS

title: Task agents that extract, map and validate data from documents and spreadsheets
problem: Advisory teams extract information from documents and spreadsheets and move it into target formats by hand.
approach: PwC said in March 2025 it used Agent OS with 250 task agents across tax, assurance and advisory (self-reported; a count only).
Data Bridge agents extract data from Excel files or PDFs, map it to a target format and validate values.
The source does not describe human checkpoints; exceptions and validation failures would need an owner.
who: PwC

title: Benchmark-stage agent that reads a whole data room and drafts the memo
problem: A full data room can hold tens of millions of tokens, more than one model reads at once; Harvey's standard agent loop read under 1%.
approach: Harvey describes a root agent dividing the data room, sub-agents reviewing each part, and a cited memo; no customer is named.
On 50 synthetic data rooms, mean pass rate rose from 23.3% to 62.4% with the decomposition harness (vendor-published).
Deal lawyers review the memo and decide what the findings mean for price, structure, representations and indemnities.
who: Harvey (benchmark; no named customer)

title: Reusable matter templates where agents run tasks and a named reviewer approves
problem: Each new matter's process is rebuilt by hand, lawyers brief the AI and track status manually, and supervision of multi-step AI work is not settled.
approach: Harvey announced Legal Work Orchestration on 2026-10-15; tasks and notifications are rolling out, templates in early access.
Each task carries scope, inputs and a reviewer; an agent can produce a consent matrix, and the partner approves before continuing.
No usage results yet; Harvey forecasts agents taking on an additional 20% of workflow steps in six months (vendor-published forecast).
who: Harvey, Certinia

title: Lawyers hand multi-file tasks to general-purpose agent workspaces, with risk-sized checkpoints
problem: Work spanning agreements, emails, meetings and files makes lawyers carry context between tools, while professional duties require supervising anything an agent produces.
approach: Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and Microsoft announced legal packages in 2026, some in preview, for multi-file tasks such as chronologies and term comparison.
Simmons & Simmons' Peter Lee describes an agent reading a file, identifying issues and drafting an advice note from a solicitor's goal.
Lawyer supervises outputs, with checkpoints around higher-risk actions. The Law Society reports very limited use of fully autonomous agents (independent).
who: Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Simmons & Simmons

title: Legal engineers and practice teams package know-how into playbooks, vaults and agents
problem: A firm's best precedent and review standards sit with a few experts, and each lawyer prompts AI from scratch, so results vary.
approach: Hogan Lovells Cadwalader built custom agents and playbooks; Blank Rome built a brief-bank vault; MinterEllison seconded staff into a legal-engineer accelerator.
MinterEllison identified more than 150 use cases; Hogan Lovells Cadwalader piloted Legora with over 1,300 lawyers (vendor-published, counts not results).
Practice experts own and update playbooks, and champions test tools on real matters before wider release.
who: Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, Blank Rome, MinterEllison

title: In-house lawyers build workflow agents for recurring assessments such as privacy reviews
problem: Recurring assessments such as data protection impact assessments and non-compete checks consume legal time for each business request.
approach: Dentsu's in-house lawyers built a Harvey agent for data protection impact assessments and workflows for non-compete checks.
Harvey's case study says the agent cut process time by 75%, without stating what was timed (vendor-published).
Dentsu reports 93% weekly use and an estimated 4 to 10 hours saved per lawyer weekly (vendor-published).
Lawyers review assessment outputs; Dentsu describes AI as supporting, not replacing, the work.
who: Dentsu, Harvey

title: In-house legal teams make AI the first pass on routine work
problem: Corporate legal departments must do more with the same team and cut outside counsel spend, yet routine drafts used to go to outside counsel.
approach: TC Energy set a 'Harvey-First' directive in its pilot, then deployed Harvey widely; GE Aerospace, Dentsu and BMW Group also use it.
JLL's general counsel recalls a solid draft in five to ten minutes (self-reported recollection, not a tracked metric).
A Harvey-commissioned survey found 48% of in-house teams mandated AI for their law firms; only one reported cost savings (vendor-published).
In-house lawyer edits and approves the first pass; complex matters stay with senior lawyers.
who: TC Energy, GE Aerospace, Dentsu, BMW Group, JLL

title: Shared AI workspaces where clients, co-counsel and advisers use the same material
problem: Drafts, diligence analysis and regulatory work pass between client, law firm and advisers by email and version control, losing context at each handoff.
approach: Harvey Shared Spaces gives internal teams and outside parties one workspace with a shared vault, workflows and permissions.
O'Melveny deploys it with clients and Dentsu shares a vault with law-firm partners; Deutsche Telekom and Gleiss Lutz are exploring it.
Participants describe fewer handoffs; none publish measures (self-reported). Each organisation's lawyers review output; the matter owner sets permissions.
who: O'Melveny, Dentsu, Deutsche Telekom, Gleiss Lutz, PwC

title: Firm expertise packaged as multi-step agents, used internally and offered to others
problem: High-value matter types such as filing analysis, fund formation and loan review need multi-step reasoning, and the know-how sits with senior lawyers.
approach: A&O Shearman and Harvey announced agents for antitrust filing analysis, cybersecurity, fund formation and loan review, for internal use and external sale.
Bloomberg Law reports plans to sell tools to other firms; Kirkland & Ellis launched a private-funds tool with Palantir.
A&O Shearman says agents do in minutes what took hours (self-reported); no product, price or external customer is published. Lawyers review outputs.
who: A&O Shearman, Harvey, Kirkland & Ellis, Fried Frank

title: Gated AI rollout: written policy, approved tools, training first, human review
problem: AI output looks complete, so reviewers may accept it untested, professionals use unapproved tools when approved ones fall short, and policy and training coverage varies by firm size.
approach: Written AI policy, approved tools, training before access, a human-review rule and independent citation checks; Reed Smith requires AI certification for associates.
ILTA survey of 508 firms: formal GenAI policy ranged from 57% (under 50 lawyers) to 98% (350-699) (independent).
Thomson Reuters survey: 34% of professionals use AI tools their organisation has not sanctioned (vendor-published).
A partner or committee approves tools and policy; humans review AI-assisted work with periodic re-checks.
who: Reed Smith, ILTA, Thomson Reuters

title: Test AI tools on the firm's own work against an expert baseline
problem: Vendor claims are hard to compare and have been overstated, reading every output removes the time saving, and relying on an untested tool breaches the competence duty.
approach: The firm tests tools on a sample of its own tasks against a lawyer baseline, relies on them only where they pass.
Vals study built with eight law firms: lawyer baseline beat the best tool on redlining, 79.7% against 65.0% (independent).
A Covington & Burling case study on document review found prompt refinement improved some issues but not all (self-reported).
Innovation lead and practice partner approve the test set and pass threshold; a lawyer decides whether to rely on the tool.
who: Reed Smith, Covington & Burling, PwC Legal, Vals

title: Idea: log edits and overrides on AI-assisted work to evidence quality
problem: Idea, not a deployment: clients want proof that AI cut cost or improved quality, and without records of corrections a firm cannot tell whether tools or people need changing.
approach: Idea. Tools would log which tasks used AI, how much output was edited or rejected, and what review found.
Thomson Reuters Institute proposes tracking override and challenge; Microsoft reports how many Legal Agent suggestions users kept (vendor-published).
No firm publishes acceptance, edit, override or rework rates. Review leads watch trends; finance and innovation leads decide what clients see.
who: No named deployment

title: Record AI use per matter and apply each client's AI terms
problem: Clients and regulators want to know when AI shaped a deliverable, and client guidelines conflict: some require AI use, others bar it or refuse to pay for it.
approach: Matter records capture where AI was used and how it was verified; deliverables carry a disclosure when AI materially shaped the analysis.
Client AI terms drive tool access and billing from matter opening; Public Services and Procurement Canada requires suppliers to flag AI use.
ILTA survey: firms requiring client approval for AI use ranged from 8% to 38% by size (independent).
Responsible partner confirms client AI terms and the engagement lead approves disclosure wording.
who: Public Services and Procurement Canada, ILTA, Deloitte Australia
